utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Mr. Robinson, with respect to the two associated exhibits, the English translation of which were uploaded last night, the Chamber has reviewed them and is of the opinion that one of which could be admitted. 65 ter number 24780B, which is a VRS IBK original log-book, we can admit two pages which were actually admitted in the Tolimir case. So shall we assign the number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit D4131.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As regards 1D29064, which is a chronology of events of the BiH army, in light of the fact that witness stated that he could not comment on that document, Chamber is of the opinion that it is not dispensable and inseparable part of the transcript so we will not admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And we hope that we won't make you do any last-minute reviews of these untranslated documents in the future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Edgerton. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may, Your Honours, I've just been updated with some information from Mr. Reid. The 65 ter number 24780B which Your Honours have just admitted, what we had noticed, and we will double check but I just wanted to put this on the record, we had noticed that the uploaded English translation didn't actually quite correspond with the dates that were discussed in the Tolimir case. And overnight, we had that additional page translated so that the English translation actually does correspond now, and we've uploaded that as an English translation under 24780B -- A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I don't follow. Additional pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, what we saw was uploaded as the English translation for that document didn't, in terms of the date entries in the log-book, correspond with what was actually discussed in the Tolimir case. So what we did was have that additional page that corresponded with the date of the 15th translated and uploaded, but that just happened sort of at speed yesterday. All that to say the English translation now completely corresponds with what was discussed in the Tolimir case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we can use the A document?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, today I'm going to ask you to have a look at some of your previous evidence that was recorded during your interview with the ICTY in 2010, and some of the evidence you gave earlier this week in the prosecution of General Mladic. Now, your interview, your audio-recorded interview with the ICTY in 2010, with respect to that, when you appeared earlier this week in the Mladic case, you were asked about that interview, whether at that time you told the truth. And you said yes. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So maybe we could have a look at the transcript of that interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it's 65 ter number 25602. And once it's called up, I'd like to go to page 33 in English and page 31 in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Todorovic, when you were asked in your interview: "Do you remember where you were when you received or when you got information that Srebrenica fell?" Which you see on the page in front of you, and you answered: "At the corps command. We had a daily briefing between 6 and 8 p.m., where what was done the previous 24 hours was discussed and also what has to be done the following ..." When you gave that answer, that was true, right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll go through a number of pages of this transcript, Your Honour, and then just deal with them all at once, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony in the Mladic case yesterday, which, if we want to look at the pages in English, is 65 ter number 25704, and pardon me, not yesterday, earlier this week, in your testimony in the Mladic case at transcript page 19821, you were asked how long after that corps command meeting where you heard about the fall of Srebrenica you received the order to prepare for the prisoners. And I'll read this to you very slowly. You said: "Looking back to that time, it's difficult for me to say if it was 1900 hours, 2000 hours of the day, or in the morning of the following day. At any rate, soon. There was an order that followed, or the order that followed soon thereafter." And then the question came: "So when you refer to 1900 hours or 2000 hours, you're referring to the evening of the corps command meeting when you learned of the fall of Srebrenica?" "A. Yes, I meant that day. Actually, it could only have happened at the time the briefing ended and when I went to my office, which was about 100 metres from the briefing room, and that was when the telegram could have been on my desk. It could have been 2100, 2200, or perhaps at some point the following day." So when you gave those answers to those questions earlier this week, in front of another Chamber of this Tribunal, you were telling the truth, right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And to go back to your interview -- and we will just go back and forth between those two documents for a sec. To go back to your interview again - 65 ter number 25602, English page 36, and B/C/S page 33 - in your interview, with respect to your task, you explained: "The point was that we were supposed to prepare the hangars for that many people who were about to arrive the following day." So when you said that, you were telling the truth; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the following day, or the following days. It depends on how it was translated. In any case, it was a little while later.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, in fact, you told the Mladic Trial Chamber on Monday of this week that the order was urgent. And at transcript page 19821, the page we just saw, you said: "Preparations had to be done as soon as possible because they would follow soon after in a day or two," referring to the prisoners. So what you told the Mladic Trial Chamber was true; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just staying on your interview --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could go over to page 41 in English and page 39 in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So here, in your interview, when you were asked where you contacted General Tolimir, you said it was at the Main Staff by phone via a three-digit number. That's true; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, I said that the number was possibly 317. However, later on, I was shown a document with a different number. This refreshed my memory that the numbers were actually 165 and 168.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, we've just talked about how you told the Mladic Chamber earlier this week that the matter of the arrival, the prospective arrival of the prisoners at Batkovic was urgent. But it's also correct - and if you like, we could look at the page in the Mladic transcript, which is 19826 - it's also correct that despite the urgency, guard reinforcements at Batkovic were never requested, were they?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said this, with this regard: Some of the preparations were completed, or actually they were on the way. The cereals were taken out and the hangar was emptied, and the rest of the preparations would ensue. Amongst that was water supply, toilet facilities, security, however that was interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's right. What I'll do to help you is I'll tell you what you told -- I'll remind you what you told the Trial Chamber in the Mladic case. You were asked the question, could military policemen be engaged without your proposal to the corps commander, and your answer was this: "In principle, I was supposed to make that proposal, but in urgent situations or when things are developing quickly, the camp warden could request a reinforcement of 20 to 30 soldiers. But we never actually got to that point because all activity was halted in that regard." That's true, what you told the Mladic Trial Chamber, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is precisely what I was going to tell you but then you interrupted me and read it out to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we could go back over to your interview, in February 2010, and look at page 46 in English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Ms. Edgerton, your question was -- previous question was whether it's correct guard reinforcements at Batkovic were never requested. Were you referring to this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could -- yes. Page 46 in English, 44 B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your interview, you were asked, and you see it on the page in front of you, why General Simic would call the brigade commander from a different corps instead of calling the corps commander, and that was after finding out that prisoners weren't coming, and you said: "Well, the relationships at that time were not all perfect or professional, so that was the time when the commander of the Drina Corps was to be replaced. So Zivanovic was supposed to step down and Krstic was supposed to become the commander of the Drina Corps. So the relationships were not that great." So that answer is also true, the answer you gave in February 2010; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was my assumption as to why things were the way they were. Pandurevic and the Zvornik Brigade were the unit adjacent to the East Bosnia Corps, our first neighbours, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not clear about this situation. What is this event referring to? If you could clarify with the witness. Simic calling from where to who.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely. Your indulgence for just one second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In your --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could go over to English page 38 of the interview, and unfortunately I don't have the B/C/S corresponding page reference handy.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At this page in the interview, Mr. Todorovic, you gave evidence that you were instructed by your commander, Simic, to check with Tolimir about when prisoners were going to arrive. And you called and had the conversation with Tolimir that I just asked you about, which you said -- when you said you spoke with him at the Main Staff and Tolimir instructed you to stop the preparation. Now, you said: "Maybe that same night or in the morning of the following day, General Simic called the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, Pandurevic, and asked him if he had any captured people in this area, so -- and if so, he could send them to me, to Batkovic." That's true; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we flip back over to page 46, you were asked why Simic would call the brigade commander, and you offered that, at that time, the commander of the Drina Corps was to be replaced. So Zivanovic was supposed to step down and Krstic was supposed to become the commander of the Drina Corps. That happened on 13 July 1995, didn't it? The handover?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About that time. I'm not sure of the date because it happened in a different unit, but in any case, that was approximately the time when that happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this telephone call between General Simic and Pandurevic happened the same day you received -- you made the telephone call to Tolimir at the Main Staff, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After I informed General Simic that the prisoners would not arrive, although they had been announced, he had a problem, and he had the idea to do what he did. He called Pandurevic, perhaps five minutes or perhaps an hour, two hours, after he had received that information. It's very difficult to be sure about the timing of events after such a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm just going to ask you one last question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. When you said, Mr. Todorovic, General Simic called Pandurevic, do you mean say that General Simic talked to Pandurevic in person or he called just Zvornik Brigade command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not there. I was not present during that conversation. After that conversation, General Simic asked me to come to his office and he told me the following: "I have just spoken with Pandurevic," he said, "And he told me that in his area of responsibility, there were people and they were members of the BiH army who could be taken prisoners because they were withdrawing in the direction of Tuzla." And then General Simic ordered me to do what you can read in the transcript, and that was to convey his order to the battalion commander, the commander of the battalion of the military police, to send a dozen or so of military policemen and the necessary number of lorries with tarpaulins who would receive prisoners and bring them back to Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you by any chance know where Pandurevic was at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see it and I didn't know. I suppose in the area covered by his unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: One last question related to the evidence you gave to Mr. Stojanovic during your cross-examination in the Mladic case, and that's at transcript page 19872. You were asked whether you were at any moment, regarding General Mladic, whether you were at any moment under the impression that General Mladic, and this was referring to 1995, had any kind of ambition to carry out a putsch. And your answer was: "I never had that impression. Quite the contrary. He was modest and carried out his duties in a strictly military fashion." That's also true; right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, then, Your Honours. Thank you, Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, just one, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember, witness, Colonel, whether in the end of July, there were any exchanges of prisoners from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't ask a single question about exchanges whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then I withdraw it. I won't insist. I'll deal with it through someone else. Thank you, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The chairman of the commission for exchanges can give you a precise answer about that. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Well, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Todorovic. On behalf of the Chamber, and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for your expediency. Thank you very much. I wish you pleasant holidays that are upcoming.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if I could just deal with the exhibits, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could add, please, pages 33 in English and 31 in B/C/S to the transcript pages that were exhibited as associated exhibits, I'm sorry, there was likely a provisional P number or D number assigned to those pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're referring to the interview?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless the parties have agreed which pages should have -- should be admitted from the interview, which were dealt with in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we assign the number for now? The number has been -- yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That we could add these pages to it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4134, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So page 33 will be added.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And page 46 in English and 44 B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Those two pages, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the circumstances, the hearing is adjourned. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00, or shall we -- can we begin with the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the problem is that the witness has to be brought from the Detention Unit and his lawyer has to be also rounded up. I don't think that we will have time for that. I also think the examination-in-chief will consist only of the -- bringing his statement into evidence, nothing more, so we wouldn't save that much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wasn't going to rise on this point, but as I indicated to Mr. Robinson yesterday, it was my understanding of the courtroom practice that when the -- when there are substantial last-minute additions to the statements, that that evidence is normally led live so that may add to the time involved. That's been the practice. It appears to me that the -- well, I don't think there is any way to argue against the fact that these additional 12 pages or so represent something much more than an insubstantial addition. So I think we have that issue to deal with as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that would be useful to deal with that issue right now so that we don't waste time tomorrow because, first of all, those additions are adjudicated facts that were laid out to the witness and the witness rebutted them. And it's not been our practice, as far as I know, that we are required to lead live additions to the statements made during the proofing with Dr. Karadzic, and we would consider that to be an unfair penalty that would implicate the equality of arms. So we would prefer, if the Prosecution was genuinely not ready to cross-examine tomorrow, that the cross-examination of the witness take place at a time when you believed they have had a reasonable time, not penalise us by depriving us of calling other witnesses by wasting court time leading things live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Wherever we may be heading but the Chamber is concerned about the last-minute change of the statement. Please bear that in mind in the future. Yes. Mr. Tieger, would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, I don't think there is any implications to the equality of arms. I think it applied across the board. Secondly, Mr. Robinson may want to characterise it as some kind of penalty, but I think the point was that there are rules for the 92 ter submissions, and if there is a failure to -- and in some respects an ongoing failure -- to fulfil those terms, then the answer is to resort to the normal way of presenting evidence. I think that's the way the Court's viewed it. And clearly no, in our submission, equality of arms issues. Actually, my recollection is that the Court was and certainly would have been as concerned with -- had -- to the extent a similar approach was used or misused by the Prosecution. So I think it's -- the question is whether or not the rules have been fulfilled and that's always available to the Defence. I also note that this witness was asked about adjudicated facts before, so it's not as if this was something that only occurred to the Defence or only could have occurred to the Defence at the last minute. The draft statement that existed before addressed adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before the Chamber rises to consider the issue but I'd like to know whether, just in case, the examination-in-chief could start sometime today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. But I would like to be heard on this issue, if you -- so that you have a full picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you may recall that at some point Dr. Karadzic was -- decided that he wanted these adjudicated facts to be in these statements so that we could clearly rebut adjudicated facts, and when the Chamber was making its deliberations, it would know clearly what adjudicated facts we were rebutting. And we started that practice of doing that here in The Hague because the investigators hadn't included adjudicated facts in the statements that they take in the field, and we, at the same time, gave instructions to the investigators to start to incorporate adjudicated facts into the statements and they started doing that and, in fact, they did that with this witness. But unfortunately, what they did with this witness was they only asked him about the adjudicated facts for Prijedor and didn't ask him about the adjudicated facts for Omarska which is where most of his information comes from. So when we saw that, it was necessary to improve that by asking him those questions when he arrived in The Hague. He's incarcerated and we don't have free access to him in Bosnia. So that's why it was done. But the issue about equality of arms is that we have investigators in the field who are essentially policemen who are doing the job that they do and we don't have the kind of -- we have maybe 20 per cent of the staff that the Prosecution has. If you look at the Prosecution's witness interviews that form the basis of 92 ter statements they were always at least one, sometimes two lawyers, present during those interviews to take the statements, make them the way they want to. For us, we can't do that. We don't have the resources to send lawyers like myself to the field and take statements like the Prosecution does, and as a result, the product that we get from our investigators isn't always as good as what the Prosecution is able to produce. And so that's what I meant by equality of arms. So I think that we deserve some flexibility and consideration for that. And we are very concerned that if we have to lead things like that live, let's say it takes half an hour or 45 minutes, we could call two other witnesses in that time and we are being deprived of that, unless you want to give us additional hours for our Defence case. So for all of those reasons, we would prefer that if the Prosecution is genuinely found by the Chamber to be unable to begin its cross-examination based on this new material, that the remedy be that they be given more time to prepare. Just like the remedy for all their disclosure violations was to give us more time to prepare, not to cost them any additional hours in their case or to exclude any evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I really don't want to have the last word but I just feel like this is something that needs to be said. To assert that the failure to ask the commander of the Omarska camp about adjudicated facts related to Omarska is an equality of arms issue is not correct. It's simply an issue of attention and care in the most simple, simplistic way. So I don't want to rub it in, but I think that's really an assertion that can't stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will rise for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has reviewed the statement, revised statement, and is now of the view that the addition is so substantial and significant, and as a consequence, following our practice, the added part should be led live by the Defence. So I'll ask the Registry how quickly the witness, next witness, could be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Something that might influence the timing, I think we will not lead those paragraphs live. We have other witnesses from Omarska, we will have those witnesses rebut the adjudicated facts, and we will give more time to the Prosecution for cross-examination on those issues that way, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then there is no need to bring in the witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It seems like that would probably be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't at the moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we confident that we can finish his evidence tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you've given three hours for cross-examination which would leave another hour and a half for redirect and some direct. We can make provisions to sit until 3.00, just to be sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. In the circumstances, the hearing is adjourned for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 29th day of November, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.06 a.m.,
